problems.statement: The ED length-of-stay rise for admitted patients is an inpatient flow problem: ED boarding grew from 1.4 h to 4.4 h because medical-ward discharges moved later in the day, so beds are not free when ED admissions need them in the afternoon.

The hospitalist rounding change of 2 March 2026 (09:30 start after a teaching meeting, new admissions first) is the root cause of the late discharges. Boarding stepped up in March-April, medical wards alone shifted, and surgical wards did not.

ED nurse understaffing is the cause of the length-of-stay rise (the client's explanation). Productive hours per visit, vacancy, grid compliance and volume are flat or better, and 3.0 of the 3.2 h increase sits in the boarding interval, which is timestamped independently of nursing.

Boarding raises the ED nurses' effective workload (inpatient care in ED rooms, fewer rooms for new patients). That explains the nurses' sense of being overwhelmed, the lower workload scores and the higher intent to leave. It is a downstream effect, not the original cause.

The ED front-end deterioration (door-to-provider 22 to 34 min, left-without-being-seen 1.6% to 3.4%) is driven mainly by boarded patients occupying rooms. The 1 May 2026 end of provider-in-triage may add to it. The relative contributions cannot be separated because there are no monthly or hourly series.

The September 2026 cut in evening bed-cleaning attendants (six to four) is making afternoon and evening boarding worse. Boarding was already about 4.2-4.4 h from April, so this is at most a minor addition, and turnaround data are missing.
Rising demand, acuity, admission rate, inpatient length of stay, or lower inpatient capacity explains the change.

Early discharge is not a rounding-start problem alone. The 4 West huddle (discharge-first list prepared in advance, case manager involvement) lowered boarding without moving the 08:00 meeting or the 09:30 start. This shows the effect comes from the order of work and the discharge preparation, not simply from restoring the 07:00 start.

actions.action: Extend the discharge-first huddle (likely-discharge list prepared the afternoon before, patients seen first, orders written before noon) to all four medical wards. Train every hospitalist in it, so it no longer depends on which of three trained physicians is rounding.
actions.rationale: It targets the established bottleneck and has quasi-random pilot evidence of roughly halving boarding for 4 West beds, without undoing the teaching meeting.

actions.action: Make discharge-before-noon and boarding-hours measures per ward visible weekly to hospital leadership and the hospitalist group. Negotiate with the Hospitalist Medical Director a round order that sees likely discharges first within the 09:30 structure.
actions.rationale: The cause is a scheduling and process choice with a trade-off (hospitalist retention) that needs an agreed fix, not a return to 07:00.

actions.action: Reframe the board paper and the CNO scorecard narrative around boarding and inpatient discharge flow, and report boarding separately from ED work-up time.
actions.rationale: The board is being asked to fund the wrong fix, and the scorecard measure mixes the ED and inpatient intervals.

actions.action: Restore the 4 West huddle if it has been paused. Do not float the charge nurse away from it.
actions.rationale: Pausing the only intervention with evidence of effect to add afternoon ED hours addresses a symptom and removes the working fix.

actions.action: Fund the $1.46M travel-nurse contract by deferring the two medical-ward case manager hires and reassigning the 4 West case manager.
actions.rationale: Case managers are part of the discharge process the pilot relies on, and coverage is already below target (1:22 against 1:15). The deferral would worsen the real bottleneck.

actions.action: Approve eight travel nurses for the ED as the main response.
actions.rationale: Staffing is at grid and productive hours per visit are flat, so extra nurses would not clear boarding. At most a small targeted boarding-hold or afternoon-surge arrangement could be considered later.

actions.action: Reinstate provider-in-triage cover (11:00-23:00), or an afternoon equivalent, once the front-end trends are shown by hour.
actions.rationale: Its discontinuation may add to the longer waits and walkouts, but there is no monthly or hourly data to separate it from the boarding effect.

actions.action: Restore bed-turnaround reporting and review the evening cleaning cut.
actions.rationale: This is an unmeasured possible additional bottleneck, but it began after boarding had already risen.

actions.action: Address ED nurse retention and workload strain directly (morale, flexible support during afternoon boarding peaks).
actions.rationale: Intent to leave is rising and that risk is real, but it is a consequence of boarding and will not be fixed by staffing alone.

nextEvidence: Hourly and monthly door-to-provider and left-without-being-seen series, with a bed-request-to-bed-ready breakdown, to separate boarding crowding from the loss of provider-in-triage in May.
Bed-cleaning turnaround times by hour after the July migration and since the 1 September cut, to see whether evening bed readiness is a second bottleneck.

Huddle-day versus non-huddle-day results on the other medical wards once the protocol is extended, together with hospitalist views on workable round-order options, to test whether the effect holds and whether it is sustainable.
output.summary: The rise in ED length of stay for admitted patients is a boarding problem, not an ED staffing problem. Of the 3.2 h increase, about 3.0 h is boarding, while nurse hours, vacancy, grid compliance, volume and acuity are flat. Boarding rose after the March 2026 hospitalist rounding change (09:30 start, new admissions first), which pushed medical-ward discharges to the afternoon. Surgical wards did not change. The 4 West huddle pilot, with schedule-determined assignment, roughly halved boarding. ED nurse strain is real but is a consequence. Do not buy travel nurses, defer case managers or pause the huddle. Extend discharge-first huddles to all medical wards.
